hookLine: Charlie and Maria Cardoso owned their house outright, and a bank's contractors still emptied it, because somewhere a clerk was signing sworn statements at a rate no human being could read.

captions.text:
On the ninth of January 2010, Charlie Cardoso
stood outside a house in Spring Hill,

Florida, and cut the padlocks off his own front
door.

He had paid a hundred and thirty-nine thousand
dollars for it, in cash,

five years earlier. There had never
been a mortgage on it.

Bank of America's crews had emptied it
the previous summer and locked him out,

and when the bank's own agent told them they
had the wrong house,
they carried on anyway.

The house they meant to take was across
the street, about ten doors down.
But nobody caught the mistake,

because catching it would have meant reading
something.
And in those same months, outside Philadelphia,

one man was signing ten thousand sworn court
documents a month,

and he was about to testify, under oath, that he
did not read them.

What happened to that one house happened, in some
form, to a country:

more than a million sworn documents manufactured
by a single company in Georgia,
filed in courthouses in every state,

and no one has ever counted how many families lost
a home because of them.
New Bedford, Massachusetts, 2005.

It starts with a couple buying somewhere to retire
to.

Charlie and Maria Cardoso lived in New Bedford,
Massachusetts,
a fishing city on the south coast.

In March 2005 they bought a three-bedroom house
with a pool at 9168 Geneva Street,
in Spring Hill, on the Gulf side of Florida,
a few blocks south of Spring Hill Drive,

in the kind of tidy subdivision where every house
has the same porch posts

and a different number. They paid a hundred
and thirty-nine thousand dollars for it.

They paid it in cash. It was Charlie's life
savings.

That word does a lot of work, so it is worth
being precise about it.

When the Cardosos paid cash, no lender
was involved.
Nobody held a lien on the place.

There was no loan to fall behind on, no monthly
payment,

and no note that anybody could sell to anybody
else.
What they got instead was a deed,
signed at a closing table and then carried

into the Hernando County recorder's office
and stamped by a clerk.

Anyone in Florida could have walked
into that building, asked at the counter,
and been shown who owned 9168 Geneva Street.

It was on the record, in the most literal sense
this country has.

The Cardosos rented the house out while they
waited to retire into it.

And in late June 2009 their tenant telephoned
in a panic.

Three men from Bank of America
were at the property to foreclose on it.

They cleaned the house out and padlocked
the doors.

Now, when a bank forecloses properly, it
is collecting a debt.

It sells the house, takes what it is owed,
and hands the rest back to the owner.
That is what makes it a debt and not a seizure.

But all of that depends on there being a debt,
and there was no debt.

Charlie Cardoso got one of them on the phone
and told him,

in the plainest words available, that he
had no loan with Bank of America,
that he had never had a loan with Countrywide,
which Bank of America had bought the year before,

and that he owned the house free and clear. He
asked the man to please double-check.

Then something happened that ought to have ended
it in an afternoon.

The real estate agent that Bank of America itself
had hired

to handle the property contacted the bank to tell
it that it was foreclosing

on the wrong home. Not the homeowner.
Not the homeowner's lawyer.

The bank's own agent, inside the bank's own
process, saying the address was wrong.

The Cardosos' attorney later put it to a reporter
this way:
their own real estate agent told them,

and nevertheless Bank of America steamrolled right
ahead.

In August, a landscaping crew working for the bank
broke the fence
to get their mowers into the yard.

Just before Christmas the tenant,
who had been frightened out of the place,
moved out for good.
And on the fifth of January 2010,

Bank of America's people came back and padlocked
the house again.
On that fifth of January,

Charlie Cardoso got through to a representative
who checked the file

and told him something
that should have been the end of it.
She said the bank had made a mistake.

She said someone would call him back within
the hour. Nobody ever called him back.
Not that day, and not on any day after it.

So on the seventh of January his son put him
in a car and drove him

from Massachusetts to Florida, thirteen hundred
miles,

because there was no longer any other way
to be heard.
He was not at the airport that week.

Maria's son was coming home from his third tour
in Iraq,
and Charlie Cardoso missed the homecoming,

because he was on an interstate going south
to argue with a padlock.

On the ninth of January the police finally agreed
to let him into his own house.

He drove to a hardware store, bought a bolt
cutter,
came back and cut every lock off the doors,

and then had to break in through the back screen
door to get inside.

The pipes had frozen because the water and power
had been shut off.
The pool pump was dead.

The lawn had brown patches where the sprinkler
system had failed

and tire tracks across it where a truck had driven
over the grass.

Almost everything they owned was gone: the air
compressor, the nail gun,

the table saw, the lawnmower, two refrigerators,
the gas grill,
and the family photographs.

The only things left were in the attic,
which the crews had apparently not found.

On the twentieth of January 2010 the Cardosos
filed suit in federal court

in Massachusetts. The bank's spokesman gave
the press a sentence that has been given
to every wronged customer in history:

the company had reached
out to their representatives and hoped

to have the opportunity to properly assess
and address their allegations.
That story sits inside a much larger number.

In 2010 alone, roughly one point two million
American homes completed foreclosure.

That was the peak year of the worst wave of home
loss since the Depression,

and in September of that year alone
about a hundred
and twenty thousand foreclosures were completed.

Every one of them was, at bottom, a paperwork
event.

Somebody produced a document asserting who owned
the loan

and how far behind the borrower was, and somebody
else acted on it.

Which raises the only question that matters
in this film,

and it is not a question about mortgages. It
is a question about reading.

Because the Cardosos were not defeated
by a computer, or by a policy,
or by a bad decision made in a meeting.
Six separate times,

a human being at that bank had the opportunity
to open a file and check an address,

and no human being did. The tenant told them.
The owner told them.
Their own agent told them.

And the machine went on producing documents
about a house it had never looked at,

because the documents were not being produced
by anyone who looked at anything.

To understand how that was possible you
have to know what the piece of paper

at the centre of a foreclosure actually is,
and what it promises,
and who is supposed to have read it.

To take a house through a court, a bank
has to hand a judge a piece of paper,
and the paper has to be sworn.

It is called an affidavit, and it is one
of the oldest devices in the legal system.
A judge cannot examine every mortgage in America.

So the law lets one person swear, on penalty
of perjury,

that they have looked at the file: that they
personally know what the loan is,

who holds it, what is owed and how far behind
the borrower has fallen.
The judge is not trusting the bank.

The judge is trusting that one named human
being sat down with the documents,

read them, and is prepared to go to prison if they
are lying.

The phrase carrying all of that weight is four
words long.

Personal knowledge of the facts. The person
swearing does not have to be important.

Usually they are not. They have to be real,
and they have to have read it.

That is the whole mechanism, and it is thinner
than it sounds,

because in a foreclosure hearing there is very
often nobody in the room

to argue back. Most homeowners in foreclosure
have no lawyer.

Many never appear at all. The affidavit is not one
piece of evidence among several.

In a great many cases it is the only evidence,
the hearing takes a few minutes,
and then a house belongs to somebody else.

So the entire structure rests on a question nobody
had thought to ask out loud.
Does the person who signs actually read them.

On the tenth of December 2009, in West Palm Beach,
Florida,

a lawyer named Christopher Immel put that question
to a man named Jeffrey Stephan.

Stephan worked for GMAC Mortgage in Fort
Washington, Pennsylvania.
He was not an executive and he was not a lawyer.

His title was team leader of the document
execution unit,
and his unit had fourteen people in it.

Under oath, Immel asked him how many documents
came to him to sign.

In a month, Stephan said, my team brings to me
approximately,

I'd say a round number of ten thousand. That's
just an estimate, of course.
Ten thousand a month.

A working month, at eight hours a day, contains
about ten thousand minutes.

He was not asked to do the arithmetic and he
did not do it.
Asked directly how long he spent on each document,
he said only that it was tough to say.

Then Immel asked the question the whole system
rests on.

So these documents wouldn't be actually executed
on your own personal knowledge?
Right, Stephan said.

There is more, and it gets worse in the specific
way that only procedure can.

The notaries who certified that Jeffrey Stephan
had appeared before them

and signed were not, he confirmed, physically
present.

In one instance in the record he executed
an assignment on the third of March

and a notary certified it on the fourth, and he
agreed that this was common.

Nobody in his unit went into the system to verify
that the figures were accurate;

they relied, he said, on the attorney network
that sent the documents in.
Six months later, on the seventh of June 2010,

a Maine lawyer named Thomas Cox deposed him again
in a second case,

and got the rest of it on the record. Four hundred
documents a day.

Do you read every paragraph of a summary judgment
affidavit before you sign it? No.
What do you read? I look for the figures.
Do you inspect the exhibits attached to it? No.

So you do not appear before the notary,
is that correct? I do not.
To be fair to the man, he did check something.

He looked at the numbers against his employer's
own computer system, though not,
he said, down to the penny.

What he did not do was read the sentence directly
above his signature,
the one that said he knew these facts personally.

The Maine court did not treat
that as a technicality.

It found the affidavit had been submitted in bad
faith and ordered the plaintiff

to pay nearly twenty-four thousand dollars
in the homeowner's costs.
When the case reached Maine's highest court,

the judges wrote a sentence that ought
to have been the end of the practice
in the United States.
The affidavit in this case, they said,

is a disturbing example of a reprehensible
practice.

That such fraudulent evidentiary filings
are being submitted

to courts is both violative of the rules of court
and ethically indefensible.
And in the same opinion, in a dissent,

a judge noted something that removes the last
possible excuse.
Four years earlier, in 2006,

a Florida court had sanctioned the very same
company for the very same practice.

It had been caught. It had been told. Nothing
had changed.

Because by then it was no longer one tired man
at one desk.
It had become an industry.

There was a building where this was done at scale,
and it looked like nothing.

A low-rise office suite in an industrial park
in Alpharetta, Georgia.
The company inside was called DocX.
It was owned by Lender Processing Services,

a publicly traded corporation headquartered
in Jacksonville, Florida,

and its business was executing the paperwork
that moved American mortgages
from one owner to another.
Between March 2003 and late 2009,

according to the United States Department
of Justice,

DocX produced more than one million fraudulently
signed
and notarised mortgage documents and filed them

with property recorders' offices across
the country.

Over those six years it took in about sixty
million dollars in revenue.

One name appears on those documents more than any
other,

and the woman it belongs to did nothing wrong.
Linda Green was real.
In 2003 she was a shipping clerk for auto parts

when her grandson told her about a job
at a company called DocX.

She told CBS she had never been a bank vice
president.
DocX made her one anyway —

a vice president of institutions she had never set
foot in —
and the reason it chose her, she said,
was that her name was short and easy to spell.

Then, as the work piled up, DocX needed more
of her.

Her name went onto hundreds of thousands
of mortgage assignments

in a dozen different hands, and she was never
charged with anything,

because the hands were not hers. One of them
belonged to a man named Chris Pendley.

In April 2011 he sat down with Scott Pelley
of Sixty Minutes and explained it

without embarrassment, because nobody at DocX
had ever told him it was wrong.

So you're Linda Green, Pelley asked him. Yeah,
Pendley said. Can't you tell.

He had been hired to sign documents using someone
else's name.

That was the job as it was described to him
on his first day.
He thought it was strange, and he said so,

and he was told repeatedly that everything
was above board and legal.

The qualification for the position was that you
had to be able to hold a pen.
He was paid ten dollars an hour.

The floor quota was three hundred and fifty
signatures an hour.

Pendley estimates he alone did four thousand
a day.

Asked how many banks he was a vice president
of on any given day, he answered:
somewhere around five to six.
There is a second person in that broadcast,
and she is the one who closes the circuit.

Shawanna Crite also worked at DocX, and she
was also a Linda Green.
She signed, and she notarised.

So if Chris Pendley was signing for Linda Green,
Pelley asked her,
you'd notarise that document. Yes, she said.

A notary's entire function is to attest
that a named person appeared before them

and signed. At DocX, the notary was at the next
desk,

certifying a signature she had just watched
somebody else invent.

You do not have to take a television programme's
word for it.

The Florida Attorney General's economic crimes
division built a presentation
on foreclosure filings, ninety-eight pages,
and put five slides in a row under one heading:
variations of the Linda Green signature.

Five scanned assignments, five different hands,
one claimed name,
each of them stamped vice president.

The deck's own summary of what it was looking
at ran:

thousands and thousands and thousands
of assignments, signed weekly.

A Florida investigator named Lynn Szymoniak, going
through her own foreclosure file,

found the name Linda Green signed as vice
president of twenty banks
at the same time.

And here is the part that makes it a public matter
rather than an office scandal.

Every one of those pages was filed with a county
recorder.

A recorder's office is the ledger of who owns what
in America —

the place a stranger goes to find
out whether a house is yours.
Once a document is recorded, it is public truth.

The factory was not producing paperwork. It
was producing title.

The machine ran until an official of Bank
of America gave a deposition

in which she said she signed seven to eight
thousand foreclosure documents a month
without reading them. Then it stopped, very fast.
On the twentieth of September 2010,

GMAC Mortgage told its brokers and agents to halt
evictions in twenty-three states.

On the twenty-ninth, JPMorgan Chase suspended more
than fifty thousand foreclosures.
On the first of October,

Bank of America froze foreclosures in the same
twenty-three states,

saying it needed to amend all affidavits in cases
that had not yet gone to judgment.

On the eighth of October it extended that freeze
to all fifty.

The number twenty-three is the whole reason any
of this ever surfaced.

In twenty-three American states — Florida, New
York, New Jersey,

Illinois among them — a foreclosure has to go
through a court,
and a judge has to be handed a sworn statement.
In the other twenty-seven,

a bank can take a house without ever showing
a judge a piece of paper.

The paperwork was only ever inspected where
somebody was legally required to look
at it. On the thirteenth of October 2010,

attorneys general from all fifty states announced
a joint investigation.
Seventeen days after it stopped, it started again.
On the eighteenth of October,
Bank of America announced its review was complete

and that it would process affidavits in a hundred
and two thousand proceedings.
On the twenty-seventh,

Wells Fargo said it would file supplemental
affidavits

in fifty-five thousand foreclosure actions. Nobody
had gone back through the files.

They had re-signed them. The reckoning arrived
on the ninth of February 2012.
Twenty-five billion dollars.

The Justice Department, the Department of Housing
and Urban Development,

forty-nine state attorneys general
and the District of Columbia —

every state except Oklahoma — against the five
biggest servicers in the country:

Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo,
Citigroup, and Ally,
which used to be GMAC.
This agreement, the Attorney General said,
is the result

of unprecedented coordination among enforcement
agencies throughout the government.

Now take the number apart, because the number
is the story.

Twenty billion of the twenty-five was consumer
relief — principal written down,

loans refinanced, credits the banks earned
by doing things to loans they still held.
Five billion was other payments.

And inside that five billion sat one fund, of one
and a half billion dollars,

and that fund was the only part of the twenty-five
billion that was cash,

in an envelope, to a person whose house
had already been taken.
One and a half of twenty-five. Six per cent.

The cheques went out in the second week of June
2013.

Nine hundred and sixty-two thousand, two hundred
and seventy-eight valid claims.
One thousand four hundred and eighty dollars each.

More people came forward than anyone had planned
for, which is its own finding —

the settlement had been sized for about three
quarters of a million.

Alongside the settlement ran a second remedy,
and it failed differently.
On the thirteenth of April 2011,

federal regulators issued consent orders
against fourteen banking organisations,

and separate orders against Lender Processing
Services and the electronic registry
that tracked who owned which mortgage.

The regulators' finding was a pattern
of misconduct and negligence related

to deficient practices in residential mortgage
loan servicing
and foreclosure processing.

The remedy was called the Independent Foreclosure
Review:

outside consultants would open every foreclosure
file

from 2009 and 2010 and find out who had actually
been harmed. They never finished.
On the seventh of January 2013,

the review was terminated and replaced
with a payment.
By the time it was cancelled,

servicers had completed final reviews
on about fourteen per cent of the files slated

for review, and not one consultant had finished
their sample.
The reason given was arithmetic:

regulators were told that finishing would cost
at least two billion dollars more
in consultants' fees,

and that the reviews themselves would return
roughly one point two billion
to the people who had been harmed.

It would have cost more to find out who was hurt
than to pay them.
So they stopped looking and started paying,

and everybody got the same thing
whether or not anything had been done to them.

The Federal Reserve's own final report says it
plainly:
the servicers were required to make cash payments

to all borrowers whose homes
were in the foreclosure process during 2009

or 2010, regardless of whether the borrower
had suffered financial injury caused
by servicer error. Here is what that produced.

The Federal Reserve published the payment table
on the ninth of April 2013.

Add up every category paid at the bottom rate
and you get two million,

three hundred and fifty-eight thousand, four
hundred and forty-one people —

out of three point nine million in the table —
who received three hundred dollars.
Fifty-nine point seven per cent of them.
At the other end,

one thousand and eighty-two borrowers received
a hundred
and twenty-five thousand dollars,

and every one of those was a servicemember
whose home had been foreclosed in breach

of a law written specifically to protect people
on active duty.
Then the cheques started coming back.

On the seventeenth of April 2013 the Federal
Reserve confirmed that people

who had received early cheques were calling
its consumer helpline

to say they had been told the cheques
could not be cashed.

The paying agent fixed it. Nobody has ever
published how many bounced.
What is on the record is a separate error:

about ninety-six thousand cheques were issued
for less than the borrower was owed,
and were corrected two months later.
And that is where the counting stopped for good.
There is no number, anywhere,

for how many American foreclosures rested
on documents that were manufactured.
Not because nobody asked —
because the only mechanism ever built

to find out was switched off with the reviews
unfinished on some eighty-six per cent

of the files. The criminal reckoning is one
sentence long.

Exactly one person went to federal prison over any
of it. Others were charged.

In Nevada, the attorney general charged two title
officers on six hundred
and six counts,

and in February 2013 a judge threw the entire
indictment out from the bench,
citing prosecutorial misconduct in the grand jury.
Neither of them was ever tried again.
Lorraine Brown, the chief executive of DocX,

pleaded guilty on the twentieth of November 2012
to conspiracy to commit mail
and wire fraud,

and on the twenty-fifth of June 2013 a federal
judge

in Jacksonville sentenced her to five years
in prison,

two years of supervised release,
and a fifteen-thousand-dollar fine.
Her company did not go to prison.
Four months before she was sentenced,

Lender Processing Services signed
a non-prosecution agreement
and paid thirty-five million dollars.

Missouri charged her too, and that case
did not begin with a regulator.

It began with a county recorder of deeds in Boone
County named Bettie Johnson,

who searched her own filing system for documents
signed with the name Linda Green —
and found them.
Two households in this story got something back,
and both of them had to go and take it.
In Naples, Florida,

a couple named Warren and Maureen Nyerges bought
a house for a hundred
and sixty-five thousand dollars in cash.

They bought it from Bank of America, because Bank
of America owned it,
because Bank of America had foreclosed on it.

About four months later, Bank of America served
them with foreclosure papers.

On the house they had just bought from Bank
of America.

With no mortgage on it, from a bank
that had been the seller.
It took eighteen months to make it go away.

The case was dismissed and a Collier County judge
ordered the bank
to pay their legal costs. The bank did not pay.

So on a Friday morning in June 2011 their lawyer,
Todd Allen,

walked into a Bank of America branch on Davis
Boulevard in Naples
with sheriff's deputies and a moving truck,

and announced that he was there to foreclose
on the bank.

Within an hour the branch manager had written
a cheque

for five thousand seven hundred and seventy-two
dollars and eighty-eight cents.

When the bank later apologised in writing, it
misspelled their name.
And Charlie and Maria Cardoso.

The bolt cutter and the back screen door got him
into the house on the ninth

of January 2010, but the argument took another
fifteen months.
In April 2011, Bank of America settled with them.

The terms were never made public, and neither side
has ever discussed them.
What is on the public record is only this:

9168 Geneva Street was theirs the entire time,
in the county's own filing cabinet,

in a document anyone could have walked
in and read.

It took a federal lawsuit to get a bank to agree
with it.

And the paper from those years is not finished
with people yet,

which is where this stops being history. So finish
the count.

Roughly seven point eight million completed
foreclosures

in the United States between 2007 and 2016,
on CoreLogic's count.

More than a million documents produced by one
company in Georgia,

signed by people who had never read them
and notarised by people sitting next
to them. Twenty-five billion dollars announced,

of which one and a half billion was cash to people
who had lost a house.
Fourteen hundred and eighty dollars each.

Two point three six million people paid three
hundred.
One person in a federal prison.

And no number at all — not an estimate,
not a range —

for how many families lost a house on paperwork
that was manufactured,

because the country stopped counting before it
knew. The paper is moving again.
Between 2006 and 2008,

the head of the Consumer Financial Protection
Bureau said in 2023,
foreclosure filings in America rose threefold,

from seven hundred thousand to two point three
million.

Many of the second mortgages written
in those years went quiet, were written off,

and were sold to debt collectors for pennies
on the dollar.
Now the collectors are back,

and the Bureau's phrase for them is zombie second
mortgages —

loans most homeowners last paid
in 2015 or earlier,

on which interest and fees have been running
the whole time,

arriving as a foreclosure threat two decades
after the ink dried.

In January 2025 the Bureau found that one or more
companies had failed

to send those homeowners the statements the law
requires.

A class action filed in Massachusetts alleges
a servicer and a trustee failed,
as a matter of systematic internal policy,

to send billing statements to borrowers
whose second mortgages had been discharged
in bankruptcy — and then moved to foreclose.

And since February 2025, in the Government
Accountability Office's own words,

the agency that wrote those findings
has been reducing the size and scope
of its activities and staffing.

Its funding cap was cut in half by statute in July
2025.

It has issued stop-work orders, closed supervisory
examinations,
and terminated enforcement cases.

Reduction-in-force notices went
to the overwhelming majority of its staff —
a plan a federal court has so far blocked,

and which is still in litigation as this film goes
out.

Somewhere tomorrow morning a page will be signed
by someone who has not read it,

and a county recorder will stamp it, and it
will become true.
That is not a prediction.
That is how the system is designed to work,
and it worked exactly as designed the last time,
which is the part nobody has ever fixed.

If you think a house somebody paid for in full
should not be able to disappear
into a filing error — and that when it does,

somebody should have to count how many times it
happened — hit like,

so the next story like this one gets told
while the paperwork is still
on the counter.
